summary: Describes a service URN to identify well-known services that depend on context, such as the user's location. Examples include emergency services, directory assistance, and call-before-you-dig lines. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5031 defines service names such as urn:service:sos to identify a type of service without tying the name to one country's phone number. A separate location-aware system can resolve the name to an address for a suitable provider.

questions: how to identify emergency services by urn
subtitle: Names a kind of service so networks can find the appropriate provider for a user's context.

tldr.problem: A familiar service number or address can vary by country or region, making it hard for a device to identify a service consistently while a user travels.
tldr.mechanism: A service Uniform Resource Name identifies a logical service, with optional sub-service labels. Separate resolution systems can map it to a locally appropriate service address.
tldr.outcome: Applications can identify services such as emergency help without embedding regional dialing details. The URN itself does not specify the resolution protocol.

today: RFC 5031 is a Proposed Standard defining the public, global service URN namespace and its initial registrations.

sections.title: A Name for a Service, Not a Number
sections.content:
Well-known services such as emergency response are provided by different organizations in different regions. The number used to reach one may not mean the same thing in another place.

The service URN gives applications a stable, location-independent way to identify the requested service. The URN identifies the logical service, not the network address of a particular provider.
sections.plainLanguage: A service name can stay the same even when the organization or address that provides the service changes by location. This lets an application request a kind of service without knowing the local number.

sections.title: The Service Name Structure
sections.content:
A service URN uses the service namespace followed by a top-level service label and, optionally, sub-service labels separated by periods. For example, urn:service:sos.police identifies a more specific service than urn:service:sos.

Labels use letters, digits, and hyphens, and are specified in lowercase. Removing labels from the right produces a valid, more general service name. Labels are assigned through the IANA registry rather than invented independently by each application.
sections.plainLanguage: The name starts with a general service and can add more specific labels after it. For example, a name can identify emergency services generally or a specific emergency service.

sections.title: Resolving the Name to a Provider
sections.content:
Service URNs are not routable addresses. A SIP proxy or user agent must resolve a URN to an address that can reach a provider in the caller's location.

The RFC expects a location-to-service mapping protocol to perform this task, but leaves the resolution protocol outside its scope. It also leaves the conversion of local dial strings into service URNs to the end host.
sections.plainLanguage: The URN says what service is wanted, not where to send a network request. Another system must use context such as location to find a routable address.

sections.title: Registered Services and Sub-Services
sections.content:
The RFC registers the top-level sos and counseling services, along with initial sub-services. The sos service is for emergencies requiring an immediate response; counseling services provide advice and support without requiring an emergency response.

New top-level labels require Standards Action. Rules for adding sub-services are defined by the document for each top-level service, including expert review for the initial emergency and counseling service families.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry starts with emergency and counseling service names. Adding new top-level service names requires a standards process, and each service family sets its own rules for sub-services.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The URN is an identifier and does not itself reveal a particular service instance. However, carrying the name in a signaling protocol can reveal what kind of service a caller wants.

Protocols that carry service URNs need their own security protections. The mapping system also needs to address threats associated with service resolution; this RFC does not define those protections.
sections.plainLanguage: A service name can reveal the type of help a caller is seeking. The protocol that carries it and the system that resolves it need appropriate security protections.
